findings.detail: 1 evidence classification violation(s) downgraded by registry

D1 [criteriaAssessments C2 mechanisms; C2 weaknesses[3]; edgeCasesAndFailureModes[0]; K12-K14] New text in C2 mechanisms and the K12-K14 scenarios applies the 'two proxies per hop' doubling only to node-proxy mode. E5 (sources/internal-loadtest-2026-10.md) reports both modes in one 'Added p99 latency per hop' column. There are two ways to read that column. (i) It counts one proxy traversal. Then sidecar, which the draft itself says has proxies on both the client and server side of every hop, should be doubled as well, giving 2.6 x 2 x 5 = 26 ms. (ii) It counts one service-to-service hop. Then the node-proxy figure already includes both node proxies on a cross-node call, unless the test only measured same-node calls. The two-proxy node-proxy scenario is only coherent under a third reading: same-node test traffic against cross-node production traffic. The draft never states this reading. The pessimistic node-proxy figures (9.0 and 10.8 ms) are still worth raising, but the asymmetry should be explained. The sidecar conclusion does not change, because doubling only makes sidecar worse.

D2 [verdict fallbacks (3) and (4); alternatives[4]; practicalImplications[3]] The new strict-case fallback (4) prefers Lattice sidecar over Portcullis plus go-spiffe/SPIRE when sidecar passes an end-to-end test. The only reason given is central R1 enforcement. It does not weigh that sidecar leaves R2 unmet while the Portcullis route covers it, or the C4 burden of each route. Fallbacks (3) and (4) also choose Portcullis plus go-spiffe/SPIRE when sidecar fails R3, calling its risks 'unquantified but not known failures'. In-app Go TLS still adds handshake and encryption cost on every one of the 5-6 hops, so R3 is unverified for this route too. practicalImplications asks for end-to-end tests of node-proxy and sidecar only, not of the in-app route. The draft should say that the in-app route also needs an end-to-end R3 test before it is adopted.

D3 [verdict] The verdict has grown into one very long paragraph. It mixes the recommendation, four combined readings of the latency headroom, a definition of 'one option' and a four-level fallback ladder, some of whose branches have their own sub-branches. The decision is still there, but a decision-maker would struggle to pull out the primary recommendation and its two gating conditions. Splitting it into a short headline recommendation, the gating conditions and a separate fallback list would fix this.

openDecisiveGaps: What is the measured end-to-end added p99 (edge plus full checkout chain) for Lattice node-proxy and sidecar modes, and for the in-app go-spiffe route if it stays a fallback, at production peak rps with 6-40 KB payloads and the actual edge component?
In the internal load test, does 'per hop' mean one proxy traversal or one service-to-service call, and were the node-proxy calls same-node or cross-node? Does R3 mean 5 or 6 proxied segments?
Will the auditor accept Lattice node-proxy mTLS (per-workload identity, rotation, STRICT enforcement, credential custody in a shared proxy) as meeting R1?
Is the one-option limit firm, would SPIRE count as a second option, and does product need R2 before the June 2027 audit?
What added p99 does Lattice ingress (or the existing edge) contribute, and does it support per-tenant limits and API keys?
